title: Seagate FireCuda Forge Pairs Your Own SSD With a Big Hard Drive for Speed
excerpt: The first drive on Seagate's Alkemi platform moves your most-used files to fast storage automatically — 8TB at $699 and 20TB at $899, SSD not included.
body:
• Seagate's FireCuda Forge pairs a high-capacity hard drive with a user-supplied NVMe SSD in one external box, using its new Alkemi platform to keep the files you use most on the fast drive automatically.
  • Seagate rates it at up to 2,500MB/s reads and 2,000MB/s writes, on Windows 11 or macOS 26 and above.
  • It is on sale now at $699 for 8TB and $899 for 20TB — but the SSD is not included, so buyers must budget for their own NVMe drive.
  • The hard drive inside is upgradeable; swapping either drive later requires a full backup and restore because Alkemi treats the pair as one volume.

Seagate has launched the FireCuda Forge, an external drive that tries to give gamers and creators SSD speed and hard-drive capacity in a single box. The Forge is the first product built on Seagate's new Alkemi intelligent storage platform, the company announced in its Business Wire release.

How Alkemi works

The idea is dynamic caching. Alkemi learns how your data is used in real time and automatically prioritises recent and frequently accessed files on a fast SSD, while the large hard drive holds the full library, according to Seagate. The Forge combines a user-provided NVMe SSD with its own high-capacity hard drive and onboard processing in a single enclosure. As The Verge notes, hybrid drives are not a new idea — Seagate has sold drives with built-in flash for years — but the Forge lets users choose and replace the components themselves.

Speeds, systems and price

Seagate rates the Forge at up to 2,500MB/s read and 2,000MB/s write performance, and says it is designed for Windows 11 and macOS 26 and above. It is available now through Seagate's online store and authorised partners in 8TB and 20TB configurations, starting at $699 for 8TB and $899 for 20TB, with availability varying by market.

The catch: bring your own SSD

The headline price is not the whole price. The NVMe SSD required for the Forge to work is supplied by the user, and with memory prices elevated, that adds meaningfully to the total cost, as The Verge points out. The hard drive is upgradeable, and users can replace either component — but because Alkemi moves data between the two dynamically, they cannot be treated as independent volumes, and replacing one means a full backup and restore first. It is also direct-attached storage, not a NAS: it connects to one computer rather than serving a home network.

Who it is for

Seagate is aiming at people whose game libraries and video projects have outgrown a single SSD but who still feel hard-drive load times daily — editors keeping current projects fast while archives sit on cheap capacity. Whether the premium over a plain external hard drive makes sense depends on the price of the SSD you pair with it, which Seagate leaves entirely in your hands.

Seagate is pitching the Forge against a backdrop of fast-growing personal data libraries: its release cites IDC's Global DataSphere Forecast, 2026-2030, on the growth of stored data. The company's bet is that buyers would rather teach one box to juggle speed and capacity than keep migrating projects between a small fast drive and a large slow one. The Forge's success will turn on whether Alkemi's file placement is invisible in daily use — if users notice the hard drive at all, the concept has failed on its own terms.
nri_angle: For diaspora creators storing large family video archives and game libraries, the Forge is a one-box option — but budget for the separate NVMe SSD it needs to work.
author: Diaspora Desk
